---
paths:
  - "cluster/manifests/**/*.yaml"
  - "cluster/applications/*/manifests/**/*.yaml"
---

* Each manifest directory contains `.registry.yaml`, auto-generated by `armyknife registry generate <manifest-directory>`. When creating a new manifest or changing pod labels (`matchLabels`), regenerate rather than manually editing: `armyknife registry generate cluster/manifests/{app}`
* Production manifests in `manifests/`, development in `skaffold/`
* Use singular resource type with underscores (`service_account.yaml`)
* Pin images by digest in kustomization.yaml, not by tag
* When using external images, add mirroring workflow as `.github/workflows/99_mirror-{image-name}.yaml` (do not reference external images directly)
* In kustomization.yaml `images` section, set `name` to match the image reference in manifests (what Kustomize searches for), `newName` to the actual registry path (what Kustomize replaces with)

## Verifying Changes Against Live State

Before adding or expanding a change to fix a problem, confirm it against the running cluster.
Do not apply a fix inferred from a past report or a known failure pattern without checking that it still applies now — the cluster changes, so a fix needed during one incident may be a no-op later.

Require both before applying:

| Confirm | How |
|---------|-----|
| The problem exists now | Reproduce live, or cite recorded evidence that still holds: `kubectl` events, container `lastState` (`OOMKilled`, exit code), Prometheus/Mimir metrics, operator/controller logs, Cilium drops (`cilium monitor`, `cilium bpf policy get`) |
| The change resolves it | Observe the behavior change (e.g., toggle the NetworkPolicy and watch the pod recover), or trace the datapath |

* When confirmation is impossible until a rare event (rolling upgrade, CNI restart), do NOT auto-apply — record it as a hypothesis and get human approval.
* Removing an unconfirmed earlier change is always allowed without this confirmation.
* Do not codify a pattern into a rule without this confirmation.

## Image References

| Image Type | `name` | `newName` |
|------------|--------|-----------|
| Internal (this repo) | `ghcr.io/hippocampus-dev/hippocampus/{app}` | `ghcr.io/hippocampus-dev/hippocampus/{app}` |
| External (mirrored) | Original image name (e.g., `nginx`, `redis/redis-stack`) | `ghcr.io/hippocampus-dev/hippocampus/mirror/{original}` |

When adding, moving, or removing an internal image reference, update the corresponding GitHub Actions workflow:

1. Find the workflow: `grep -l "{image-name}" .github/workflows/00_*.yaml`
2. Update `env.KUSTOMIZATION` with repository-root-relative path(s) (comma-separated, no spaces)

## Secret Management

When a Deployment references a Secret (via `envFrom.secretRef` or `env.valueFrom.secretKeyRef`), ensure the Secret is properly configured:

| Secret Source | Required Configuration |
|---------------|------------------------|
| Vault | Create `secrets_from_vault.yaml` in `overlays/dev/` |
| ConfigMapGenerator | Use `secretGenerator` in `kustomization.yaml` |

SecretsFromVault is an exec plugin.
When running `kustomize build`, always pass `--enable-alpha-plugins`:

```
kustomize build --enable-alpha-plugins <path>
```

For Vault secrets, add `secrets_from_vault.yaml` to `kustomization.yaml` resources:

```yaml
# secrets_from_vault.yaml
apiVersion: kustomize.kaidotio.github.io/v1
kind: SecretsFromVault
metadata:
  name: {app-name}
spec:
  vaultSecrets:
    - path: /kv/data/{app-name}
      key: {SECRET_KEY}
```

Example: `cluster/manifests/cortex-api/overlays/dev/secrets_from_vault.yaml`

## Container Defaults

* Consistency with existing patterns takes precedence over minimizing fields
* When adding fields, check similar files in the repository and match their style
* When defining a new container `resources` block, always specify `requests` (Kubernetes copies `limits` into `requests` when `requests` is omitted, handing the scheduler the limit as the reservation); `## When to Define Resources` decides whether the block exists at all and which of `requests`/`limits` it carries - match a field to the reader or enforcer its row names
* All containers require secure defaults (non-root UID 65532, no privilege escalation, read-only filesystem, `emptyDir` uses `medium: Memory` for small writable temp/cache; use default `emptyDir: {}` for volumes that may grow unboundedly such as logs, plugins, or application data to avoid counting against the container's memory limit); mount runtime socket volumes under `/run/` and temporary data volumes under `/tmp/` (not at root-level paths like `/sock` or `/backing`)
* Set `dnsConfig.options` with `ndots: "1"` to prevent unnecessary DNS search domain expansion (all services use FQDNs, not short names like `service.namespace`). The path varies by workload type:

| Workload | dnsConfig Path |
|----------|----------------|
| Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet | `spec.template.spec.dnsConfig` |
| Job | `spec.template.spec.dnsConfig` |
| CronJob | `spec.jobTemplate.spec.template.spec.dnsConfig` |
| Istio Gateway (IstioOperator-managed) | Via `overlays` patches in `cluster/bin/deploy-istio.sh`, not Kustomize |

Exception: node-local-dns uses `dnsPolicy: Default` for node-level DNS caching, reached through a `CiliumLocalRedirectPolicy` rather than from the node's own network namespace
* Use `restricted` Pod Security Standard by default; use `baseline` or `privileged` only with documented reason in namespace.yaml comment
* All workloads require standard labels (`app.kubernetes.io/name`, `app.kubernetes.io/component`). Exception: utility base manifests use only `app.kubernetes.io/component` (see `utilities.md`)
* When avoiding hardcoded values: use Kustomize (replacements, configMapGenerator) for cross-resource references, Downward API for own pod metadata (name, labels, resources), scripts/API calls as last resort (example: `cluster/manifests/utilities/redis/` and `cluster/manifests/translator/overlays/dev/redis/kustomization.yaml`)

## Cache Directory Redirection

Under `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true`, libraries that cache to a home-relative default (e.g. `$HOME/.cache/{tool}`) cannot write.
A single library often has several independent cache locations, so redirecting only the primary one can still crash — enumerate them from the library's docs.

| Approach | When |
|----------|------|
| Redirect each cache env var to a writable volume (`/mnt/.cache/{tool}`) | Library exposes a cache-path env var |
| Mount a writable volume at the default path (`$HOME/.cache/{tool}`) | Library has no override env var |
| Disable the cache-writer feature | Its cache is a separate location that cannot be cleanly redirected (e.g. incompatible with the volume type) |

| Volume type | When |
|-------------|------|
| NFS | Model/data cache reused across pods |
| `emptyDir` | Ephemeral per-pod cache |

Examples: `cluster/manifests/whisper-worker/overlays/dev/patches/deployment.yaml` (HuggingFace hub cache redirected; the separate xet cache disabled rather than redirected, being ill-suited to the NFS volume), `cluster/manifests/embedding-retrieval/base/deployment.yaml` and `cluster/manifests/memory-bank/base/deployment.yaml` (`FASTEMBED_CACHE_PATH`), `cluster/manifests/cortex-api/base/deployment.yaml` (mount-based, multiple tool caches)

## Pod Metadata (Labels and Annotations)

Pod metadata is defined in `pod.metadata` within deployment/statefulset/daemonset specs.

### Istio Sidecar Injection

When a workload needs Istio sidecar injection, add the label and proxy resource annotations to `pod.metadata.labels` and `pod.metadata.annotations`:

```yaml
spec:
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        sidecar.istio.io/inject: "true"
      annotations:
        sidecar.istio.io/proxyCPULimit: 1000m
        sidecar.istio.io/proxyMemoryLimit: 1Gi
        sidecar.istio.io/proxyCPU: 10m
        sidecar.istio.io/proxyMemory: 64Mi
```

| Annotation | Value | Purpose |
|------------|-------|---------|
| `sidecar.istio.io/inject` | `"true"` | Enable Istio sidecar injection |
| `sidecar.istio.io/proxyCPULimit` | `1000m` | CPU limit for the proxy container |
| `sidecar.istio.io/proxyMemoryLimit` | `1Gi` | Memory limit for the proxy container |
| `sidecar.istio.io/proxyCPU` | `10m` | CPU request for the proxy container |
| `sidecar.istio.io/proxyMemory` | `64Mi` | Memory request for the proxy container |

Values in the table are baselines.
Deviate only when measured proxy usage requires it, and add an inline comment on the annotation stating the reason (e.g., `# Use proxy-wasm`).
Read the deviating workloads for the values in effect rather than assuming a figure.

Omit these annotations if the namespace has `istio-injection=disabled` label or if the workload must run without a sidecar (e.g., `hostNetwork: true` workloads are incompatible with Istio sidecar).

Examples: `cluster/manifests/bakery/overlays/dev/patches/deployment.yaml`

### Istio Resource workloadSelector

When creating Istio resources (PeerAuthentication, Sidecar, Telemetry) for multi-component services (e.g., DaemonSet + StatefulSet, multiple Deployments), use only `app.kubernetes.io/name` in `workloadSelector` to apply the policy to all components with a single resource:

| Service Structure | workloadSelector Labels |
|-------------------|------------------------|
| Single component | `app.kubernetes.io/name` (optionally with `app.kubernetes.io/component`) |
| Multiple components sharing same policy | `app.kubernetes.io/name` only |
| Multiple components with different policies | Separate resources per component with both `name` and `component` |

Examples: `cluster/manifests/kube-state-metrics/overlays/dev/sidecar.yaml` (applies to both DaemonSet and StatefulSet)

## Container Field Order

Container fields must follow this order (omit fields not needed):

```
name → securityContext → image → imagePullPolicy → command → args → env → resources → ports → startupProbe → readinessProbe → livenessProbe → lifecycle → volumeMounts
```

Probe fields follow this order:

```
exec/httpGet/tcpSocket → initialDelaySeconds → periodSeconds → successThreshold → failureThreshold → timeoutSeconds
```

## Runtime Resource Detection and cgroup

Rust (tokio) and Go runtimes determine worker thread count based on detected CPU cores.
Without proper configuration, the runtime may spawn threads for all node CPUs, causing excessive context switching when the container is throttled.
The JVM sizes its heap the same way, from detected memory.

**Applies to Go, Rust, and JVM workloads**, including upstream images.
Check `cluster/applications/{app}/Dockerfile` for in-repo applications:
- Go: `FROM golang:*`
- Rust: `FROM rust:*` or `FROM ghcr.io/rust-lang/rust:*`
- JVM: the container entrypoint runs `java` (upstream images often do — check the workload rather than assuming)
- Not applicable to CPU/heap auto-sizing: `nginx`, `python`, `node` — but a native proxy still needs its own connection cap, see `.claude/reference/cluster/manifests/native-daemon-limits.md`

Only the bullets keyed on an entrypoint resolve for an upstream image; the rest need a Dockerfile this repository owns.
Where there is none and the entrypoint resolves none of the bullets above, the language is not established, so record the container for a human rather than concluding it is none of these.

| Language | Required Configuration |
|----------|------------------------|
| Go | `resources.limits.cpu` + `GOMAXPROCS` env via `resourceFieldRef: limits.cpu` |
| Rust (tokio) | `resources.limits.cpu` (cgroup quota auto-detection) |
| JVM | Bound the heap — see `.claude/reference/cluster/manifests/jvm-heap.md` for the three approaches |
| Native daemon | Explicit connection cap in its own config — see `.claude/reference/cluster/manifests/native-daemon-limits.md` |

### Go

In `base/deployment.yaml`, define ONLY the GOMAXPROCS/GOMEMLIMIT env vars (no resources section):

```yaml
env:
  - name: GOMAXPROCS
    valueFrom:
      resourceFieldRef:
        resource: limits.cpu
  - name: GOMEMLIMIT
    valueFrom:
      resourceFieldRef:
        resource: limits.memory
```

Do NOT write `GOGC` to state the default.
`100` is the *Go runtime* default, not necessarily the application's — an application that calls `debug.SetGCPercent` or ships its own default reads the env var as an override, so writing `100` silently discards that tuning.
Scrape `go_gc_gogc_percent` from the running workload before writing any value — observed defaults in this cluster differ per application, so the number must come from the metric rather than from the Go documentation.

Set `GOGC` in `overlays/dev/patches/` only where measurement justifies lowering it.
The ceiling on what a lower `GOGC` reclaims is the drop in peak committed heap, computed against the value actually in effect — not against 100.
Only the resident part of that is returned, so check `go_memstats_heap_released_bytes` against `go_memstats_heap_sys_bytes`: a workload whose scavenger has already given the pages back has nothing left to reclaim.

In `overlays/dev/patches/deployment.yaml`, define ALL resources:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: {container-name}
    resources:
      requests:
        cpu: 10m
        memory: 64Mi
      limits:
        cpu: 1000m
        memory: 128Mi
```

The `resourceFieldRef` works at runtime (Kubernetes reads limits from the final merged manifest), not at Kustomize build time.
Patches merge into base before deployment.

`GOMAXPROCS` is sourced with no `divisor`, and a divisor-less CPU `resourceFieldRef` rounds up to whole cores, so what the container sees is `ceil(limits.cpu)` and the value moves only when that ceiling changes.
`1000m` to `500m` leaves it at 1 while the CFS quota halves, but `1000m` to `1500m` moves it 1 to 2 and `2000m` to `1000m` moves it 2 to 1, so compare the two ceilings rather than looking for an integer between the endpoints.
Where the ceiling does move, the circularity clause in `.claude/reference/cluster/manifests/deriving-resource-values.md` governs instead, and it withholds the change altogether rather than merely redirecting where the number comes from.

Sourcing `GOMEMLIMIT` from `limits.memory` makes Go's soft limit equal the hard cgroup limit, so the transient overshoot Go permits above the soft limit lands on the OOM killer instead of triggering a GC.
Size `limits.memory` with headroom above the observed peak `container_memory_working_set_bytes`, not at it, and read sibling Go workloads' `requests`/`limits` for the prevailing spread rather than assuming a fixed ratio.
When the observed peak already sits against the current limit, the circularity clause in `.claude/reference/cluster/manifests/deriving-resource-values.md` governs instead, and it withholds the raise altogether rather than merely redirecting where the number comes from.

### Rust (tokio)

Set `resources.limits.cpu` to enable cgroup-based detection via `available_parallelism()`, which reads the CFS quota:

```yaml
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 5m
  limits:
    cpu: 1000m
```

`requests.cpu` sets the cgroup weight and leaves the quota unset, so a container carrying a request alone detects the node's full core count.
`available_parallelism()` rounds that quota down and clamps it at one, so the `1000m` above yields a single worker thread and `2000m` two — the opposite direction from the Downward API's `ceil()` in `### Go`.
Before introducing a quota on a workload that has none, see `## When to Define Resources`.

## OpenTelemetry Environment Variables

When adding OpenTelemetry tracing to a container, include all required environment variables.
Do NOT add only a subset.

### Common (all languages)

| Variable | Value Pattern |
|----------|---------------|
| `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` | `http://otel-agent.otel.svc.cluster.local:4317` |
| `OTEL_SERVICE_NAME` | Downward API: `metadata.labels['app.kubernetes.io/name']` |
| `OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER` | `parentbased_traceidratio` |
| `OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG` | `"1.0"` |
| `OTEL_BSP_SCHEDULE_DELAY` | `"5000"` |
| `OTEL_BSP_EXPORT_TIMEOUT` | `"30000"` |
| `OTEL_BSP_MAX_QUEUE_SIZE` | `"2048"` |
| `OTEL_BSP_MAX_EXPORT_BATCH_SIZE` | `"512"` |

### Go only (add after common variables)

| Variable | Value Pattern |
|----------|---------------|
| `OTEL_GO_X_EXEMPLAR` | `"true"` |
| `OTEL_METRICS_EXEMPLAR_FILTER` | `trace_based` |

Example: `cluster/manifests/reporting-server/overlays/dev/patches/deployment.yaml` (Go), `cluster/manifests/embedding-gateway/overlays/dev/patches/deployment.yaml` (Python)

## Container Ports

* Always specify `name` for containerPort (Service's `targetPort` references by name, not number)
* Always specify `protocol: TCP` explicitly (even though it's the default)
* Define `metrics` port only if the application exposes its own metrics endpoint (Istio sidecar metrics via port 15020 don't require containerPort definition)
* Declaring one port number under both TCP and UDP leaves the list with duplicate strategic-merge keys — `ContainerPort` merges on `containerPort` and `ServiceSpec.ports` on `port`, neither of which includes `protocol` — so ArgoCD's client-side apply can never converge once such a list changes: the live object keeps a mix of old and new entries, the Application stays OutOfSync forever and selfHeal recreates the pod on every reconcile, which makes the live port list something to reconcile by hand rather than by resync
* Reconcile such a diverged live port list by replacing the whole array with `kubectl patch --type=json` (a JSON Patch `replace`, not a strategic merge) — the live object then matches what the Application already renders, so selfHeal has nothing left to revert

| Port Name | Purpose |
|-----------|---------|
| `http` | HTTP service |
| `https` | HTTPS service |
| `grpc` | gRPC service |
| `metrics` | Prometheus metrics (containerPort only; use `http-metrics` for Service ports — ValidatingAdmissionPolicy requires `^(grpc\|http\|tls\|tcp\|udp)` prefix) |

## Service Link Environment Variables

Kubernetes injects `{SERVICE}_PORT=tcp://{ip}:{port}` and friends into every container for each Service in the namespace, uppercasing the Service name and replacing `-` with `_`.
An application that reads a configuration variable of the same name receives a URL where it expects a bare value, and the collision surfaces only once the Service exists — the container starts fine in isolation.

Set `enableServiceLinks: false` on the pod spec whenever a Service in the namespace mangles into a prefix the application itself reads — compare `{SERVICE}_PORT`, `{SERVICE}_SERVICE_HOST` and `{SERVICE}_SERVICE_PORT` against the application's configuration keys, not only against its documented environment variables.
Almost every destination here is reached by FQDN, so add the field against a confirmed collision rather than as a default on new workloads — and check the container's own arguments first, since `cluster/manifests/node-local-dns/base/daemon_set.yaml` names a Service in `-upstreamsvc` and resolves it only through `KUBE_DNS_UPSTREAM_SERVICE_HOST`, where turning the links off would leave the whole cluster without DNS.

Example: `cluster/manifests/seata/base/stateful_set.yaml` (the `seata` Service injects `SEATA_PORT`, which seata reads as its own listen port and fails to parse as an integer)

## Topology Spread Constraints

When using `matchLabelKeys` in `topologySpreadConstraints`, use the correct label for each workload type:

| Workload | matchLabelKeys | Reason |
|----------|----------------|--------|
| Deployment | `pod-template-hash` | Auto-generated by ReplicaSet controller |
| StatefulSet | `controller-revision-hash` | Auto-generated by StatefulSet controller |

Using the wrong label causes `matchLabelKeys` to be ignored (the label does not exist on pods).

## When to Define Resources

Define `resources` in `overlays/dev/patches/` only when one of the following conditions is met (for operator-managed CRs such as TidbCluster, define resources directly in the CR spec using the same conditions):

| Condition | Reason | Example |
|-----------|--------|---------|
| HPA configured | HPA requires `resources.requests.cpu` to calculate scaling metrics | bakery, embedding-gateway |
| Go `resourceFieldRef` | `GOMAXPROCS`/`GOMEMLIMIT` reference `limits.cpu`/`limits.memory` at runtime | exactly-one-pod-hook, gateway-proxy |
| Non-Go `resourceFieldRef` | A cache size or proxy count references `requests.memory`/`limits.cpu` at runtime | memcached, varnish, redis |
| Rust (tokio) | `available_parallelism()` reads the cgroup CPU quota, which only `limits.cpu` sets | connectracer, fluentd-delayed-unlink |
| JVM heap bounded by percentage | Without `limits.memory` the heap ceiling falls back to a share of node memory | knative-eventing-kafka |
| JVM heap derived by an operator from a CR | The operator computes `-Xms`/`-Xmx` from the CR's own `resources`; with none set the heap ceiling falls back to a share of node memory | knative-eventing-kafka, mimir |
| Unbounded growth with no in-process cap | Nothing reads `limits.memory` — it is the cap itself, enforced by the kernel's OOM kill | realtime-search-exporter, argocd |
| Namespace carries a `ResourceQuota` constraining `limits.*` | A pod that omits the constrained field is rejected at creation | jupyterhub |
| Upstream defaults diverge from observed usage | Upstream ships resources that are too large (causes contention in dev) or too small (risks OOMKill) relative to actual observed usage | knative-eventing-kafka, mattermost |

If none of these conditions apply, do not add `resources` to the patch.
When adjusting existing resource values, do not add `resources.requests` or `resources.limits` to containers that do not already have them set — except on a JVM workload whose heap is bound by `resources`: introducing `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage` on a container requires adding `limits.memory` alongside it, and an operator that derives `-Xms`/`-Xmx` from a CR requires `requests` and `limits` in that CR (see `.claude/reference/cluster/manifests/jvm-heap.md`).
A tokio workload carrying `requests.cpu` alone has the same shape, since adding `limits.cpu` is what creates the quota `available_parallelism()` reads rather than an adjustment of a value already there — but record that one for a human instead of applying it, because introducing a quota drops the worker count from the node's full core count to that quota rounded down, never below one.
In `overlays/dev/patches/`, when only one field (e.g., `requests`) needs correction and upstream already provides acceptable values for the other (e.g., `limits`), patch only the diverging field — Kustomize strategic merge will preserve the upstream values for unpatched fields.
This does not hold for operator-managed CRs, where defaulting is typically per block (all-or-nothing on `requests`/`limits`) — restate the upstream values being kept, and confirm the operator's defaulting granularity in its source before omitting a field.
A Knative Service holds its `resources` in the ksvc's own `spec.template.spec.containers[]` wherever its `service.yaml` lives, because the Revision's Deployment is controller-generated and no Deployment patch can reach it.
When overriding upstream defaults, add a comment on the container entry indicating the upstream values being overridden (e.g., `# Override upstream defaults (requests: cpu 200m, memory 450Mi)`).
Whenever the number comes from a metric rather than from an upstream default, read `.claude/reference/cluster/manifests/deriving-resource-values.md` before writing it.

## HPA-Managed Workloads

When a workload has a HorizontalPodAutoscaler (HPA), do NOT include `replicas` field in Kustomize patches.
ArgoCD selfHeal reverts HPA scaling changes when the patch defines an explicit replica count.

| HPA Configured | Kustomize Patch |
|----------------|-----------------|
| Yes | Do NOT include `replicas` field |
| No | Include `replicas` field |

Example: `cluster/manifests/fluentd/overlays/dev/patches/stateful_set.yaml` (HPA manages replicas, patch omits `replicas`)

## Rolling Update Strategy

Use an integer for `rollingUpdate.maxUnavailable`, not a percentage.
Percentages round down for Deployment and StatefulSet (`20%` of `replicas: 1` = `0`), which blocks rollouts because the controller cannot tolerate any unavailable pod and refuses to terminate the only existing pod.
Default to `1`; `0` is acceptable when paired with `maxSurge: 1` for zero-downtime Deployment rollouts.

| Workload | Path |
|----------|------|
| Deployment | `spec.strategy.rollingUpdate.maxUnavailable` |
| StatefulSet | `spec.updateStrategy.rollingUpdate.maxUnavailable` |

DaemonSet's `maxUnavailable` rounds up, so percentages remain safe and are not subject to this rule.

Pair `minReadySeconds` with a `failureThreshold` above `1`.
The availability window restarts from the Ready condition's transition time on every flap, and a StatefulSet has no `progressDeadlineSeconds`, so a probe that trips on one slow response stalls the rollout with no error at build or sync time.

## resizePolicy

Only add `resizePolicy` when VPA (VerticalPodAutoscaler) with `updateMode: Auto` is configured for the workload.

| VPA Configuration | resizePolicy | Manual resource adjustment |
|-------------------|--------------|---------------------------|
| `updateMode: Auto` | Required | Do NOT adjust — VPA continuously overwrites `resources.requests` and `resources.limits` based on observed usage |
| `updateMode: Off` / No VPA | Do not add | Adjust normally |

To check whether a workload is VPA-managed: look for `vertical_pod_autoscaler.yaml` in the workload's manifest directory or its sub-directories.

Example: `cluster/manifests/utilities/minio/` (has both `vertical_pod_autoscaler.yaml` and `resizePolicy` in `stateful_set.yaml`)

## Pod Security Standards

| Level | When to Use | Comment Required |
|-------|-------------|------------------|
| `restricted` | Default for all namespaces | No |
| `baseline` | NFS volumes, GPU workloads, Istio Gateway/Waypoint, Strimzi Kafka, specific runtime requirements | Yes |
| `privileged` | eBPF, host network, Kaniko/Docker-in-Docker | Yes |

When using `baseline` or `privileged`, add a comment in `namespace.yaml` explaining the reason:

```yaml
labels:
  # whisper-worker uses nfs
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: baseline
```

### Capabilities

Do not add Linux capabilities that are unnecessary in Kubernetes:

| Capability | Kubernetes Context | Action |
|------------|-------------------|--------|
| `IPC_LOCK` | Swap is disabled by default | Do not add |
| `NET_ADMIN` | Required only for network namespace manipulation | Add only if needed |
| `SYS_PTRACE` | Required only for debugging/profiling | Add only if needed |

For `restricted` compliance, always drop all capabilities: `capabilities: { drop: [ALL] }`

## Bootstrap (postStart)

Some bootstrap work can only run once the container's own server process is listening on a unix socket or `127.0.0.1`.
An initContainer finishes before the main container starts, so it can never reach that process.

| Bootstrap needs | Mechanism |
|-----------------|-----------|
| The container's own process listening locally | `lifecycle.postStart` running `sh /mnt/init.sh`, from a `configMapGenerator` mounted read-only at `/mnt` |
| Only rendered config on disk before startup | initContainer |
| An API reachable from any pod | Job / ArgoCD hook |

postStart runs concurrently with the entrypoint and re-runs on every container restart, so the script must wait for its own precondition rather than assume readiness, and must be idempotent.
A non-zero exit kills the container, so a bootstrap that cannot yet succeed has to keep waiting rather than fail.

Examples: `cluster/manifests/vault/base/`, `cluster/manifests/mattermost/overlays/dev/`

## Graceful Shutdown (preStop)

Applications with `lifecycle.preStop` sleep allow Kubernetes Endpoints to propagate before SIGTERM processing.
However, if the application implements lameduck internally, preStop sleep is redundant.
Write an active preStop with the native `lifecycle.preStop.sleep.seconds` action, and reach for `exec` only where the hook does more than sleep — the commented-out form under `### When Lameduck is Implemented` stays as written, since it documents a hook that is not in effect.

Take the first row that matches.

| Application Type | preStop Required |
|------------------|------------------|
| Reached through a `CiliumLocalRedirectPolicy` | Yes, and it has to drop readiness rather than only sleep |
| External images (nginx, redis, etc.) | Yes |
| controller-runtime (webhooks, controllers) | Yes |
| Go/Rust/Python with internal lameduck | No |

Cilium drops a local redirect backend only when labels, pod IPs, the UID or the Ready condition change, and a deletion timestamp changes none of them, so a preStop that only sleeps leaves the terminating pod serving as a backend after it has stopped answering.
Such a preStop has to make the pod unready itself, which moves the health check the readiness probe gives up onto `startupProbe`, so nothing enters the backend list unchecked, and onto `livenessProbe`, since the Ready condition stops tracking health once the readiness probe reads a marker.
A marker file driving that readiness probe lives on a pod-scoped volume, so pair it with a `postStart` that clears it — otherwise a container the kubelet restarts inherits the marker and the pod never becomes ready again.
Size the preStop sleep above that probe's own detection window (`periodSeconds` × `failureThreshold`), since the pod stays a backend until the kubelet has observed the marker — probe timings left at their defaults outlast a short sleep, and the container then takes SIGTERM while Cilium is still sending it queries.

### Checking for Lameduck Implementation

Search for lameduck pattern in source code:
- Go: `time.Sleep(lameduck)` after `signal.Notify(quit, syscall.SIGTERM)`
- Rust: `time::sleep(lameduck)` after signal handling

### When Lameduck is Implemented

Comment out preStop and add explanation:

```yaml
          # {app-name} implements lameduck
          #lifecycle:
          #  preStop:
          #    exec:
          #      command: ["sleep", "3"]
```

Example: `cluster/manifests/bakery/base/deployment.yaml`, `cluster/applications/anonymous-proxy/manifests/deployment.yaml`

## Prometheus Metrics Scraping

When Istio sidecar is enabled (`sidecar.istio.io/inject: "true"`), Prometheus scrapes metrics via port 15020 (Istio merged metrics), NOT the application port.

| Istio Sidecar | Prometheus Scrape Port | NetworkPolicy |
|---------------|------------------------|---------------|
| Enabled | 15020 | `allow-envoy-stats-scrape` only |
| Disabled | Application port (e.g., 8080) | App-specific NetworkPolicy |

Do NOT add separate NetworkPolicy for application metrics port when using Istio sidecar.
The `allow-envoy-stats-scrape` NetworkPolicy (port 15020) handles all Prometheus scraping.

The merged endpoint on 15020 exposes application metrics only when the pod declares where to find them.
Without these annotations the sidecar serves Envoy stats alone and the application's metrics are silently absent — Prometheus reports no scrape error.

| Annotation | Value |
|------------|-------|
| `prometheus.io/scrape` | `"true"` |
| `prometheus.io/scheme` | `http` |
| `prometheus.io/port` | The application's `metrics` containerPort, quoted |
| `prometheus.io/path` | The application's metrics path |

Place them in `pod.metadata.annotations` after the `sidecar.istio.io/*` annotations.
Omit all four when the application exposes no metrics endpoint of its own.

```yaml
# Correct: allow-envoy-stats-scrape covers all pods with sidecar
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-envoy-stats-scrape
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  ingress:
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels:
              name: prometheus
          podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app.kubernetes.io/name: prometheus
              app.kubernetes.io/component: ""
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 15020
```

## NetworkPolicy Egress

The `default-deny` NetworkPolicy uses an empty `podSelector` with no `policyTypes`, which restricts ingress only.
Do NOT add `egress` rules to non-utility NetworkPolicies — adding an `egress` section implicitly activates egress enforcement, blocking all egress not explicitly allowed (including istiod xDS connections).

| Component | Egress in NetworkPolicy | Egress control |
|-----------|------------------------|----------------|
| Application pods (Deployments, CronJobs, etc.) | Do NOT add | Istio Sidecar (L7) |
| Utility pods with `policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]` (e.g., redis-peer) | Required in consumer overlay | NetworkPolicy (L4) — see `utilities.md` |

## Service-to-Service Communication

When adding or removing service-to-service communication, update both sides:

| Side | Configuration |
|------|---------------|
| Caller | Sidecar egress (+ ServiceEntry for external hosts) |
| Callee | NetworkPolicy ingress (+ AuthorizationPolicy if using Istio) |

### Istio Ambient Mesh (Waypoint Proxy)

Use Ambient Mesh when sidecar proxy is incompatible with the workload (e.g., Kaniko cannot run with UID 1337 required by istio-proxy).

When a caller uses Ambient Mesh (`istio.io/dataplane-mode: ambient`), the destination service needs a waypoint proxy.

**Callee configuration:**
1. Add `waypoint.yaml` (Gateway with `gatewayClassName: istio-waypoint`)
2. Add `istio.io/use-waypoint: waypoint` label to Service
3. Allow HBONE port 15008 in NetworkPolicy
4. Set `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: baseline` in `namespace.yaml` with comment `# {app} has a waypoint` (waypoint pods lack `seccompProfile`, which `restricted` requires)

When the destination service has `waypoint.yaml`, the NetworkPolicy must allow HBONE port 15008 in addition to the application port:

```yaml
# waypoint.yaml
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: waypoint
spec:
  gatewayClassName: istio-waypoint
  listeners:
    - name: mesh
      port: 15008
      protocol: HBONE
```

```yaml
# network_policy.yaml
ingress:
  - from:
      - namespaceSelector:
          matchLabels:
            name: caller-namespace
    ports:
      - protocol: TCP
        port: 8080
      # HBONE
      - protocol: TCP
        port: 15008
```

| Destination has `waypoint.yaml` | NetworkPolicy ports |
|---------------------------------|---------------------|
| Yes | Application port + HBONE (15008) |
| No | Application port only |

Examples: `cluster/manifests/cortex-api/overlays/dev/`, `cluster/manifests/token-request-server/overlays/dev/`, `cluster/manifests/httpbin/overlays/dev/`

### Sidecar Mode Selection

| Condition | Mode | Reason |
|-----------|------|--------|
| All destinations are known cluster services | `REGISTRY_ONLY` | Least privilege, explicit egress |
| Connects to node IPs (kubelets, host endpoints) | `ALLOW_ANY` | Node IPs are not in service registry |
| Connects to dynamic/arbitrary external hosts | `ALLOW_ANY` | Cannot enumerate all destinations |
| Manages arbitrary cluster resources (operators, dispatchers) | `ALLOW_ANY` | Destinations change dynamically |

Default to `REGISTRY_ONLY`.
Use `ALLOW_ANY` only when destinations cannot be enumerated in egress hosts.

### Sidecar Egress (REGISTRY_ONLY mode)

Use specific FQDNs for least privilege:

| Destination | Format | Example |
|-------------|--------|---------|
| Same namespace | `./{service}.{namespace}.svc.cluster.local` | `./mimir-etcd.mimir.svc.cluster.local` |
| Cross namespace | `{namespace}/{service}.{namespace}.svc.cluster.local` | `otel/otel-agent.otel.svc.cluster.local` |
| Knative Service | `{namespace}/*` (wildcard required for per-Revision services) | `alerthandler/*` |
| External host | `./external-host.com` + ServiceEntry | `./api.github.com` |

Use `./` prefix for services in the same namespace (peer communication, utility services).
Use `{namespace}/` for cross-namespace access.

Avoid `{namespace}/*` for non-Knative services - it allows access to all services in that namespace.

Take each host from the callee's own Service manifest rather than from the component name or from a sibling app's Sidecar file.
Nothing validates the string: a component whose Service is registered under another name (a headless discovery Service is its own Service), a component shipping a workload but no Service, and a namespace segment left over from the file it was copied from all pass `kustomize build`, sync clean, and match nothing at runtime.
Confirm the name against the callee's built output before adding a host, and re-confirm before treating one already present as live egress.

No `cluster.BlackHoleCluster.*` counter answers whether anything is being dropped - the cluster has no endpoints, so no upstream connection is ever attempted and every one of them stays at zero while connections are being discarded.
The drops surface as `istio_tcp_connections_opened_total` with `destination_service_name="BlackHoleCluster"` and `response_flags="UH"`, which the merged metrics endpoint exports, so query it through Grafana rather than reaching for the proxy admin endpoint.
That series collapses the destination, so confirm each expected host separately against the proxy's own cluster list - a client that fails quietly (memcached does) leaves the noisy destination named in the workload's logs and the silent one looking healthy.

### Sidecar Port Exclusion

Excluding a port from outbound capture and relaxing inbound mTLS on that same port is one change, not two, wherever the callee carries a sidecar.
Excluding only the outbound side then leaves the callee's `STRICT` policy closing the now-plaintext connection, which for a consensus protocol means the peer cannot vote.
A callee running outside the mesh has no PeerAuthentication to pair with, so there the caller-side exclusion stands alone.

| Side | Field | Value |
|------|-------|-------|
| Caller | `traffic.sidecar.istio.io/excludeOutboundPorts` in `pod.metadata.annotations` | The port, quoted |
| Callee | `portLevelMtls."{port}".mode` in `peer_authentication.yaml` | `PERMISSIVE`, with a trailing comment naming the protocol or the components that dial it; omit where the callee has no sidecar |

Exclusion is not the default for member-to-member traffic — memberlist gossip stays captured in loki, mimir, tempo and pyroscope, and etcd's raft peer port carries `PERMISSIVE` alone in `cluster/manifests/mimir/overlays/dev/etcd/`.
Exclude only where a comparable workload already does, or where capture is confirmed live to break the protocol.

An excluded port never reaches Envoy, so a Sidecar `egress` host listed only to carry it is inert and belongs out of the list.
Check the callee's other Service ports first — `egress` matches a host, not a port, so dropping a Service that also serves an unexcluded port takes that port down with it.

Examples: `cluster/manifests/seata/` (9091 raft), `cluster/manifests/mimir/`, `cluster/manifests/loki/` and `cluster/manifests/tempo/` (9095), `cluster/manifests/pyroscope/` (4040), `cluster/manifests/memory-bank/overlays/dev/qdrant/` (6335), `cluster/manifests/adhoc/elasticsearch/` (9300), `cluster/manifests/strimzi-cluster-operator/` (2181 and 9091, callee outside the mesh)

### Resource Naming

| Pattern | Resources | Example |
|---------|-----------|---------|
| App/component name only | PeerAuthentication, Sidecar, Telemetry, AuthorizationPolicy, Gateway, VirtualService | `varnish`, `cortex-api` |
| `{app}-{feature}` | EnvoyFilter, VirtualService (specific routes) | `varnish-access-log`, `embedding-gateway-purge` |
| `{parent-app}-{utility}` | NetworkPolicy, VirtualService (utility routing) | `cortex-api-redis`, `assets-minio`, `whisper-worker-redis-haproxy` |
| `{workload}-peer` | NetworkPolicy admitting the workload's own pods on a member-to-member port | `seata-peer`, `etcd-peer` |
| FQDN | ServiceEntry, VirtualService (cross-namespace) | `api.github.com`, `*.svc.cluster.local` |

Utility names match directory names under `cluster/manifests/utilities/`.
When a utility ships multiple components (the `redis` utility provides both `redis` and `redis-haproxy` pods), use the targeted pod's `app.kubernetes.io/component` instead of the directory name.

Do not use descriptive suffixes like `-allow-purge` or `-deny-external-cache-invalidation` for single-purpose resources.

### External Egress

When accessing external hosts, both Sidecar and ServiceEntry are required:

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: ServiceEntry
metadata:
  name: api.github.com
spec:
  exportTo:
    - .
  hosts:
    - api.github.com
  location: MESH_EXTERNAL
  ports:
    - name: https
      number: 443
      protocol: HTTPS
  resolution: DNS
```

Examples: `cluster/manifests/runner/overlays/dev/service_entry.yaml`, `cluster/manifests/alerthandler/overlays/dev/service_entry.yaml`

### TLS Origination

When the application sends plain HTTP and needs the Istio sidecar to upgrade to HTTPS:

| Application Protocol | ServiceEntry Port | DestinationRule | Example |
|---------------------|-------------------|-----------------|----------|
| HTTPS (application handles TLS) | port 443, protocol HTTPS | Not needed for TLS | Standard (most services) |
| HTTP (sidecar handles TLS) | port 80, protocol HTTP, targetPort 443 | `tls.mode: SIMPLE` on port 80 | Varnish → api.openai.com |

```yaml
# ServiceEntry
ports:
  - name: http
    number: 80
    protocol: HTTP
    targetPort: 443
---
# DestinationRule
trafficPolicy:
  portLevelSettings:
    - port:
        number: 80
      tls:
        mode: SIMPLE
```

Example: `cluster/manifests/memory-bank/overlays/dev/service_entry.yaml`, `cluster/manifests/memory-bank/overlays/dev/destination_rule.yaml`

## External Host (kaidotio.dev) Checklist

All external services must have `{service}.kaidotio.dev` with ext-authz.
The `-public` suffix is an **additional** domain, not a replacement:

| Condition | Hosts | ext-authz |
|-----------|-------|-----------|
| Default | `{service}.kaidotio.dev` | Add to authorization_policy.yaml |
| Needs public access | `{service}.kaidotio.dev` + `{service}-public.kaidotio.dev` | Add regular domain only |

Do not leave `{service}.kaidotio.dev` absent — it is always required.

When adding `-public`, also update `terraform/cloudflare/access.tf` and `terraform/cloudflare/main.tf` (`local.public_hosts`).

## Proxy-WASM Filters

When deploying proxy-wasm filters, prefer WasmPlugin over EnvoyFilter:

| Use Case | Choice | Reason |
|----------|--------|--------|
| Default | WasmPlugin | Simpler, fewer lines of YAML |
| Need `INSERT_BEFORE` specific filter | EnvoyFilter | WasmPlugin only supports phase-based ordering |
| Need to insert before `istio.metadata_exchange` | EnvoyFilter | WasmPlugin cannot insert before this filter |

Example: `cluster/manifests/httpbin/overlays/dev/wasm_plugin.yaml` (WasmPlugin), `cluster/manifests/httpbin/overlays/dev/envoy_filter.yaml` (EnvoyFilter)

## Sub-Component Placement

When a service depends on another component, decide whether it should be a sub-directory under the parent or a standalone ArgoCD Application:

| Relationship | Placement | Example |
|--------------|-----------|---------|
| Tightly coupled (exists only for the parent) | Sub-directory under parent's `overlays/dev/{component}/` | `memory-bank/overlays/dev/cloudevents-relay/` |
| Shared infrastructure (redis, minio, etc.) | Sub-directory referencing `cluster/manifests/utilities/` | `memory-bank/overlays/dev/qdrant/` |
| Independent service (own lifecycle) | Standalone `cluster/manifests/{service}/` with own ArgoCD Application | `bakery/` |

Sub-components share the parent's namespace and ArgoCD Application.
Each sub-component directory contains its own `kustomization.yaml`, Istio resources (peer_authentication, sidecar, telemetry), and `patches/`.

| Sub-component Type | kustomization.yaml `resources` | `namePrefix` | `labels` |
|--------------------|--------------------------------|--------------|----------|
| Utility (from `cluster/manifests/utilities/`) | `../../../../utilities/{utility}` | `{parent}-` | `includeSelectors: true`, `app.kubernetes.io/name: {parent}`, `variant: utilities` |
| Knative Service utility (from `cluster/manifests/utilities/`) | `../../../../utilities/{utility}` | `{parent}-` | `app.kubernetes.io/name: {parent}`, `variant: utilities` (no `includeSelectors`) |
| Application-specific (from `cluster/applications/`) | `../../../../../applications/{component}/manifests` | Not required (uses application's own labels) | Application's own labels |

When adding a sub-component, also update the parent's ArgoCD Application `manifest-generate-paths` annotation to include the sub-component's source directory.

Examples: `cluster/manifests/memory-bank/overlays/dev/qdrant/` (utility), `cluster/manifests/memory-bank/overlays/dev/cloudevents-relay/` (utility)

## Operator-Normalized CR Fields

Some operators register an admission webhook that rewrites a typed CR field into one canonical representation regardless of how it was written in git (e.g., tidb-operator's `spec.{pd,tikv,tidb,ticdc}.config` accepts a YAML map, an empty map, or a string, but the webhook always rewrites the live object's field to a TOML string).
Writing the field as a YAML map (or `{}`) then causes ArgoCD to show a permanent diff, because the live value never matches the git value.

Before adding `ignoreDifferences` (see `.claude/rules/cluster/manifests/argocd-applications.md`) for such a field, confirm the webhook's canonical output via a `kubectl diff` dry-run (see `## Verifying Changes Against Live State`), then write that canonical form directly in the CR with a comment recording why — this eliminates the drift at the source instead of merely hiding it from diffing.
Reserve `ignoreDifferences` for fields whose live value is unpredictable or generated by a controller (defaults, `caBundle`, etc.), where no canonical form can be written in advance.

Example: `cluster/manifests/slack-logger/overlays/dev/tidb_cluster.yaml`

## ArgoCD Sync Waves

Resource-level `argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave` annotations run on their own scale, separate from the waves on ArgoCD Application manifests in `cluster/manifests/argocd-applications/`.
Derive a resource's wave from what it depends on rather than picking a number — whatever must exist first gets the lower wave.

| Resource | Wave |
|----------|------|
| CR that another CR requires before it can reconcile (KafkaNodePool) | One wave ahead of the CR that consumes it |
| Resource reconciled against an existing CR (KafkaTopic, TidbInitializer, AtlasSchema) | One wave behind that CR |
| Job seeding a utility (minio bucket, schema) | One wave behind the utility's `kustomization.yaml` wave |

When the same CR family already exists elsewhere, read those instances and reuse the identical chain instead of deriving a new one.
Kustomize does not validate waves, so a mismatch surfaces neither at build nor at sync time — it is found only by comparing against a sibling.

## ArgoCD Application

After creating manifests for any workload, create an ArgoCD Application:
  Read: `.claude/rules/cluster/manifests/argocd-applications.md`

## Workload Types

| Workload | Description |
|----------|-------------|
| External Service | HTTP services exposed via Istio Gateway |
| Internal Service | Cluster-internal HTTP services |
| Stateful | StatefulSet for databases, caches |
| Daemon | DaemonSet for node-level agents |
| CronJob | Scheduled periodic tasks |
| Job | One-time tasks, ArgoCD hooks |
| Knative Service | Serverless HTTP (scale to zero) |
| Knative Eventing | Event-driven with Broker/Trigger |
